item.title: The Daily Star – The lonely worlds of Syed Waliullah’s fiction
item.description:
Syed Waliullah was a novelist, a short-story writer and a playwright. Though he was not a prolific writer – he has only three novels, four plays and two short-story collections to his credit – he is recognised as one of the foremost modern writers in Bangla literature, with a Bangla Academy Award to his name. This essay will discuss his fiction, in Bangla as well as in English.

His two volumes of short stories, Nayanchara (1945) and Dui Teer O Anyanya Galpa (1965), contain a total of 17 stories. However, his total number of stories may be around 50. Syed Shamsul Haq attributes about 25 short stories to Syed Waliullah. Syed Waliullah: Galpa Samagra (Jonaki Prakashani, 2021) reveals that he had 32 published stories which he did not anthologise. Ahmed Mostofa Kamal, in Syed Waliullah: Shrestha Galpa (Bishwa Sahitya Kendra, 2008), has included nine stories which were not anthologised by the writer himself. Kamal believes that perhaps Waliullah was too busy or thought the stories did not fit in with the other stories in the anthology.

Waliullah’s correspondence with Anne-Marie Thibaud – who would soon become his wife – suggests a possible reason why another short-story anthology did not soon follow Nayanchara. In a letter dated 24 November 1954, Waliullah tells Anne-Marie about a volume of short stories he was putting together. According to him, the manuscript was ready for the press: “I have collected most of them. I am now busy retouching them which I find absolutely necessary. . . . Though you will not understand the language, I will send you a proofcopy containing these titles. You can at least say if they look good” (in Anne-Marie Waliullah’s Waliullah: My Husband as I Knew Him, Nymphea, 2022).
 
Syed Waliullah in Paris, January 1965.

Waliullah believed that the manuscript would be ready for the press by Friday – that is, two days later. He had been planning to write a novel in English, but he told Anne-Marie that work on the book had to be suspended for the Bangla short-story collection. He also had to write a play of about 12,000 words for PEN. No one knows what happened to this collection of short stories, as his second short-story anthology appeared almost ten years later. The English novel he was planning was perhaps suspended permanently.

From his posting in Karachi in 1951 to his subsequent postings in Jakarta, London and Bonn, and finally to Paris in 1961, where he lived until his death in 1971, Waliullah lived away from his homeland and his Bangla-speaking milieu. However, he never forgot the land where he had spent his childhood and youth. Most of his short stories, whether in Bangla or English, are set in Bengal, though a few are set on board a boat or a ship, some in a place that could be anywhere on earth, and one in an undetermined space between two countries. Lal Salu (1948), as well as the two Bangla novels he wrote in Europe – Chander Amabasya (1963) and Kando Nadi Kando (1966) – are set in Bengal.

Almost all of Waliullah’s fiction has a sad ending. Perhaps losing his mother when he was very young left a void in Waliullah’s life, which is reflected in much of his fiction. As Anne-Marie notes in Waliullah: My Husband as I Saw Him, “This constant shift of places, which means he most likely could not make close school friends, together with the loss of his mother at the age of eight, partly explains his reserved character, his aloofness and some of his rootlessness.”
 
Cover of Syed Waliullah: My Husband as I Saw Him by Anne-Marie Waliullah (Nymphea, 2022), a personal account of the celebrated Bengali novelist’s life and literary journey.

His father’s second marriage must also have affected him. Though later in life Waliullah always visited his half-brothers, half-sisters, stepmother and step-aunt when he returned to his homeland, they could not fill the void in his life. Moreover, Waliullah’s relationship with his father was not a close one. Syed Ahmedullah could not understand his artistic son. His step-aunt relates how upset his father was when he came upon his son drawing instead of studying. He tore up the painting and pulled his son up by his hair. Waliullah quietly said, “I’ll have to cut my hair to go on painting.” The relationship between son and father may be seen replicated in different ways in his fiction, most particularly in the relationship between Mohammad Mustafa and his father in Kando Nadi Kando. Thanks to the nature of his father’s job, Waliullah got to see the small mofussil towns of Bengal, but the unhappy relationship between father and son, who showed no keenness to follow in his father’s footsteps and become a civil servant, is revealed in his fiction, as well as in what we learn from his letters to his wife and other sources.

The tone of nostalgia and gloom, perhaps what may be called an existential despair, is present in many of his stories, whether written in Bangla or English. Stories like “No Enemy” and “Cargo” – both written in English and later translated by Waliullah into Bangla – as well as “Mrityuyatra” (The Death March) reveal an existential despair, as do his later novels Chander Amabasya and Kando Nadi Kando.

Waliullah wrote only three novels in Bangla: Lal Salu (transcreated as Tree Without Roots, 1967), Chander Amabasya and Kando Nadi Kando. Lal Salu, referring to the red cloth used to cover shrines, is Syed Waliullah’s first and most famous novel. Initially published by Comrade Publishers in Calcutta, Lal Salu was subsequently published in Dhaka, East Pakistan, and continues to be published in Bangladesh.
 
The cover of the first edition of Syed Waliullah’s debut novel, Lal Salu (1948), designed by Zainul Abedin.

Lal Salu narrates the story of Majeed, who finds a neglected shrine and pretends that it is the resting place of a famous Muslim saint. Appointing himself as its guardian, he preys upon the simple villagers. He marries Rahima, a childless widow. After some years of a childless marriage, he takes a second wife, a young girl named Jamila. Unlike the docile Rahima, Jamila has a mind of her own. One day, Majeed decides to punish her and forces her to spend the night alone in the shrine. However, that night there is a violent hailstorm. When Majeed goes to the shrine to see how Jamila is, he finds her unconscious. Alarmed, he takes her to their hut and leaves her with Rahima. He then sets off to check what damage the hailstorm has caused to his crops. On the way, villagers come to him, lamenting their losses. Majeed tells them not to lose faith in God. The Bangla novel ends here, with Majeed and the villagers looking at the fields destroyed by the hail.

In 1963, Anne-Marie Thibaud’s French translation of the book, L’arbre sans racine, was published. Four years later, an English translation of the novel appeared as Tree Without Roots, with the title translated from the French. Four translators were credited: Anne-Marie Thibaud, Qaiser Saeed, Jeffrey Gibian and Malik Khayyam. However, in Waliullah: My Husband as I Saw Him, Anne-Marie describes how she had translated the book, as well as Chander Amabasya, from Waliullah’s own English translation.
 
The cover of Tree Without Roots (1967), Syed Waliullah’s English transcreation of Lal Salu, the first of his three Bangla novels.

Waliullah could not resist correcting or improving what he had written earlier. Even published pieces are marked by corrections or changes. The English translation that he had prepared of Lal Salu, so that his wife could translate it into French, was done more than a decade after he had written the novel. Apart from the change in the title, there are several other changes. Perhaps the most striking ones are in the opening and final chapters. The poverty of the land is described in vivid language: “There are too many of them on this land, this piece of raped and ravaged land which yields no more. They know it, but what can they do? Every inch of it is ploughed and sown.”

The most significant deviations of Tree Without Roots from the Bangla original are the added chapters at the end, which make Majeed a more complex character than in Lal Salu. The Damra, a quiet river which was thought to be dying, has flooded, and Majeed realises that the river has become so powerful that, at any moment, it could break its high bank and flood his hut and the shrine. He cannot leave the shrine which he has created, but at least he can save his wives. Accompanied by Rahima and carrying Jamila in his arms, he takes them to his friend Khaleque’s house and asks him to look after them. Leaving them there, he returns through the floodwaters to the shrine: “A thin, haggard man, with sunken, utterly expressionless eyes, his sparse beard as pale as the dawn, a frail human speck standing alone on the edge of a vast expanse of water that merged into the infinite vastness of the sky.”

Syed Waliullah’s second novel, Chander Amabasya, opens with the description of a moonlit scene in a bamboo grove. Aref Ali, a young teacher who happens to be there, discovers the half-naked dead body of a young woman. When he emerges from the bamboo grove, he notices a man whom he recognises as Qadir, the younger brother of Dada Sahib, the elderly man who has hired him. Though Aref Ali recognises Qadir, he cannot connect the man to the dead woman.
 
The cover of Chander Amabasya, Syed Waliullah’s second novel. It opens in a moonlit bamboo grove, where a young teacher’s discovery draws him into a moral dilemma.

Later, Qadir asks for Aref Ali’s help in burying the woman. Aref Ali thinks that the murder was an accident and that Qadir was in love with the young woman. He believes that Qadir wanted to hide the woman’s body because he was in love with her and did not want her half-naked body to be seen by people. However, when Aref Ali realises that Qadir had never loved the woman, he decides that it is his moral duty to tell Dada Sahib, his patron, as well as the police.

He does so. However, the police do not seem to believe his story. He finds himself being accused of the murder. Apart from him, there is no witness, and he is told that he has been seen committing the murder. Aref Ali ponders over the death of the young woman and thinks that someone has to be punished for the crime. Even, perhaps, he himself. As in the later Kando Nadi Kando, Chander Amabasya also asks the same moral question: How far is a person responsible for an act committed by someone else?

The river Barkal is crying.” Believing that if they give gifts to the river, it will not die, the townspeople throw whatever they can into the river: a slaughtered calf, pots, pans, clothes, rice, pulses, gold and silver ornaments.
 
The cover of Syed Waliullah’s Kando Nadi Kando, translated into English by Osman Jamal as Cry, River, Cry in 2015.

Mustafa is supposed to board the steamer on the day it does not arrive. When Mustafa returns home, he hears that his cousin, Khodija, has committed suicide. As children, Mustafa and Khodija had been pledged to each other by his father. When Khodija learnt that he was getting married to someone else, she drowned herself in the small pond behind the house. I have a feeling if it is accepted by an outside publisher, I might take a bold decision.”

This book was not The Ugly Asian, which is not about villages but about American politics in Asia. Did Syed Waliullah ever write this book? If he had written even a few pages, Anne-Marie would have kept them safe, just as she kept all his published and unpublished writings safe – something their daughter Simine is doing now.

One piece of unfinished English writing which Anne-Marie kept safe was a work very different from his other writings. Written in English, like The Ugly Asian, and, like it, under the pseudonym Abu Sharya, it is very different in tone, setting and theme from that novel. How Does One Cook Beans begins in a South Asian country but then shifts with the narrator to France. It is a humorous piece of writing, reflecting the side of Waliullah that his family and friends saw. Though there is a sort of an ending, it is unfinished. He had started writing it in 1961, but perhaps the demands of life, work and family intervened, and he could not finish it. Instead, he went on to write two other Bangla novels, Chander Amabasya and Kando Nadi Kando – both set in his homeland.

Niaz Zaman is a retired academic, writer and translator.

The refrain that Dhaka’s developmental problems are partly due to the lack of a coherent ‘vision’, despite proliferating declarations, reports and planning initiatives, is a familiar one among publics concerned with the megacity’s long-term sustainability. Researchers often attribute this to poor or non-existent coordination among state agencies in planning and policy implementation, the dominance of private real estate and rentier interests in ‘residential accumulation’, and the ubiquity of ‘corruption’ when it comes to the making and implementation of statutes in the development process, from zoning regulations to land acquisition and environmental laws. (The term ‘residential accumulation’ alludes to a compelling analytical framework developed in Javier Moreno Zacarés, ‘Residential Accumulation: A Political Economy Framework’, Housing, Theory and Society, 41(1), pp. 4–26.) 

Each of these attributes characterises Greater Dhaka’s peri-urban expansion to varying degrees. With four large municipalities and rapidly urbanising peripheries extending from Ashulia and Savar in the northwest to Rupganj (a subdistrict in Narayanganj) in the east, Greater Dhaka is now the world’s second-largest metropolitan region, with about 37 million inhabitants, just behind Jakarta but ahead of Tokyo (UN-DESA, The World’s Cities in 2025: Data Booklet, New York, 2025, p. 6).

The lament about the so-called lack of ‘vision’ or urban planning failures in Dhaka’s development is understandable. In a chaotic city where urban life appears to be governed by providential caprice and jungle law in equal measure, a ‘vision’ of order (or the lack thereof) is appealing from a humanist sensibility. Even in his arguably anti-humanist works, Marx differentiated human labour from non-human agencies by the former’s capacity to imagine a normative ideal. While the spider and the bee might put us to shame with their instinctual mastery of weaving and architecture, respectively, “what distinguishes the worst architect from the best of bees is that the architect builds the cell in his mind before he constructs it in wax” (Karl Marx, Capital, Vol. 1, translated by Ben Fowkes, London, 1990, p. 284. Louis Althusser develops his argument on the ‘anti-humanist’ strain in late/mature Marx’s theoretical works in his much-debated essay ‘Marxism and Humanism’). However, such an appeal regarding (the lack of) a coherent vision often misses the competing visions implicit in urban development schemes and the work that comparisons do within them.

Take, for example, a 2018 report published by a group of urban economists at the World Bank, titled Toward Great Dhaka: A New Urban Development Paradigm Eastward. The report claims that, with appropriate infrastructure for flood and drainage management, improved transportation, municipal consolidation and formalised property rights in a context of relative land availability, the region offers a “unique opportunity” for urban expansion eastwards, with the potential to accommodate an additional 6 million inhabitants by 2035 (Julia Bird, Yue Li, Hossain Zillur Rahman, Martin Rama and Anthony J. Venables, Toward Great Dhaka: A New Urban Development Paradigm Eastward, Washington, DC, 2018, p. 126). Besides expanding the housing stock, the authors expect the region to be an engine for economic growth and job creation as a mixed-use commercial district and logistics hub, attracting new businesses through a mix of tax incentives and reduced red tape. Such claims are based on mapping alternative spatial-economic trajectories through a series of sophisticated modelling exercises, taking the 119 square kilometres between the Balu and Shitalakshya rivers as the unit of analysis. 

Although not a planning document, the report is nevertheless one of the only comprehensive, future-oriented statements on urban development to date regarding this rapidly urbanising region in Greater Dhaka. Its imagined future is explicitly modelled on the affluent and highly urbanised Pudong district in eastern Shanghai.

But what is the report actually doing? Let us consider both its geopolitical and social dimensions. Published in 2018, the report frames Dhaka as a potential transit-logistics hub along the Asian Highway Network (AHN). Its proposals for the city’s eastern fringes are explicitly justified in these terms. While the AHN project has been around for quite some time, its renewed traction is partly due to its purported role as a counterweight to China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). The timing proves crucial. The World Bank’s relationship with the then-ruling Awami League regime remained rocky following the former’s withdrawal from financing the Padma Bridge due to corruption allegations. A Chinese state-owned company was subsequently contracted for the bridge’s construction. Chinese financial assistance and growing interest in expanding Mongla port (now connected by the bridge to Dhaka) as part of the BRI indicate an ongoing geopolitical shift. The report’s broader objectives are thus better understood as an attempt to thaw relations after the setbacks of the early 2010s.

Key assumptions underpinning the report’s analysis (e.g. relative land availability and ease of acquisition, the viability of technical-infrastructural fixes for drainage in a low-lying region, and consensual participation among current inhabitants in the coming agrarian-urban transition) lend themselves to a familiar post facto justification of conflict-ridden processes long underway. Since the city’s 1995 master plan, exercises in refining the mesh of land-use regulations through detailed area plans (DAPs) have often served as cover for land grabs, unauthorised real estate encroachments and environmental deregulation at the urban fringes (Efadul Huq and Mohammad Azaz, ‘The destructive work of restoration: Fishing communities facing territorialization in Turag river’, Environment and Planning E: Nature and Space, 7(4), 2024, pp. 1526–1554; Shahadat Hossain and Kirsten Hackenbroch, ‘Whose interest finally counts? The statutory production of urban space at the fringes of Dhaka, Bangladesh’, Planning Theory, 18(2), 2019, pp. 167–190). A colluding planning agency (RAJUK) has regularly turned land-use maps into instruments for legitimising real estate capital through the power of the rubber stamp (TM Seraj and MA Islam, ‘Detailed Area Plan: Proposals to Meet Housing Demand in Dhaka’, in Dhaka Metropolitan Area and Its Planning: Problems, Issues & Policies, Dhaka, 2014). 

In my ongoing research on urbanisation in Greater Dhaka, I examine the role of these and other processes in transforming the agrarian hinterland of its eastern peripheries into real estate property. Kanchon, a former subdistrict in Narayanganj just outside the report’s unit of analysis, on the eastern bank of the Shitalakshya River, is my case in point.
A map based on RAJUK’s Structure Plan 2016–2035 showing strategic land-use zones across Greater Dhaka, with proposed development priorities for East Dhaka, Central Dhaka, the N8 corridor and the Savar–Gazipur–Tongi region. Source: World Bank

A region bordering some of the largest state-led and private housing development projects in recent decades, Kanchon has experienced the encroachment of real estate capital over the last decade, shaped by a series of complex processes. These include agrarian-economic change, weakening socio-economic ties to the old core of Narayanganj City, and the growth of a land market accompanying the physical transformation of vast swathes of land through sand-filling operations. Land brokers, or jomir dalals, have emerged as key beneficiaries from within this agrarian-urban milieu in recent years. Such changes are reflected in the administrative redesignation of Kanchon as a municipality in 2009. Charting this transformation through the competing accounts of my interlocutors in the region, I raise questions about the report’s assumptions. For example, if acquiescence precedes acquisition, then the complex sociocultural and political-economic dynamics through which this happens undermine the supposedly easy ‘availability’ of land in Greater Dhaka. The competing visions of agrarian-urban futures that inform such a process (including the report’s) are thus important in my account. The report’s sophistication obscures its underlying support for real estate boosterism at the expense of alternatives, a concern familiar to scholars studying peripheral urbanisation in Dhaka and elsewhere.

But if the report simply justifies ongoing practices, then what kind of a ‘vision’ does it offer, if any? The comparative lens, explicit (and implicit) in the report, suggests at least three, each of which downplays alternatives that are potentially more viable and equitable. First, consider its references to Pudong in eastern Shanghai, the city’s financial district dominated by corporate offices, high-income/luxury housing and tourism. Juxtaposing this vision with eastern Dhaka mirrors the ambitions of developers and upper-middle-class homeowners, whose real estate investments would eventually be transformed into financial capital and rents in the new urban economy. A corresponding vision ‘from below’ animates the brokers and fixers working for (state and private) developers. Successful brokers experience upward mobility not only through earnings from land deals but also through vertically integrated operations that ensure the consolidation and marketability of land as real estate property, including subcontracting in the sand-filling business. 

In my work, I find that the economic prospects do not appear as certain for the majority of land sellers, including smallholding farmers and their tenants. Many experience what sociologists Shelley Feldman and Charles Geisler call in situ displacement, making do in the informal economy as petty shopkeepers, rentiers, and transport vehicle owners and operators (Shelley Feldman and Charles Geisler, ‘Land expropriation and displacement in Bangladesh’, The Journal of Peasant Studies, 39(3–4), 2012, pp. 971–993. Feldman and Geisler invoke this type of displacement especially in the context of urban peripheries). Some procure work as enforcers and subcontractors for prominent land brokers. Outmigration among semi-proletarian household members for supplementary wage work in Dhaka and Narayanganj cities also continues.

If the World Bank report was serious about transforming the region into a transit-logistics hub, then the realities on the ground would suggest Shekou rather than Pudong as the more appropriate ‘model’. The region’s historical ties to the river port of Narayanganj and the industrial hub to its north could have formed the basis of a future economic corridor. Improved transit and logistics, including better connectivity to the country’s major seaports, could be envisioned to support a more diversified urban economy centred on manufacturing that serves both export and domestic markets. The Djibouti City–Addis Ababa corridor, modelled on the port-park-city development pioneered by Shekou on the outskirts of Shenzhen in the late 1970s, thus offers an alternative comparison. This major industrial-transit corridor in the Horn of Africa is part of China’s BRI, where Shekou served as the ‘home template’ (see Xiangming Chen, ‘Building Away from a Home Template: China's Role in Reshaping the Urban-Industrial-Logistical Landscapes Spanning a Djibouti-Ethiopia Corridor’, Asian Perspective, 50(1), 2026, pp. 23–49). The report’s failure to consider such alternatives may reflect the influence of geopolitical frameworks that limit which models of urban and regional development are considered appropriate and valuable.

Second, consider the report’s seemingly practical suggestion regarding an important ecological-infrastructural intervention: building and modernising embankments along the Balu River, a tributary of the Shitalakshya. Since the river has historically been responsible for inundating large swathes of land during the monsoons, embankments are seen as essential for urban development in this low-lying region. Here, I am reminded of urban researcher Fahmid Ahmed’s prescient question regarding water management in Dhaka: to flow or to fortify? (Fahmid Ahmed, To Flow, or to Fortify? In the intervening years since the report’s publication (and Ahmed’s research), rapid real estate encroachment in the region has resolved this question in favour of ‘fortify’, without, of course, solving the problems of drainage and severe waterlogging. Chronic problems of waterlogging in the privately developed Bashundhara Residential Area, and repeated fiascos regarding infrastructural investments to retrofit its inadequate drainage networks, are well known.

However, even in 2018, the embankment issue was somewhat of a red herring. The report’s ecological-infrastructural ‘vision’ could have been informed by this history, or by the histories of other ‘soaking ecologies’, as the environmental historian of Calcutta’s urban development, Debjani Bhattacharyya, puts it: histories in which urbanity is imagined through the erasure of rich agrarian lifeworlds, often with devastating social and ecological consequences (Debjani Bhattacharyya, Empire and Ecology in the Bengal Delta: The Making of Calcutta, Cambridge, 2018).

The third and final dimension of the urban future envisioned in the World Bank report makes a familiar move, regarding the region’s agrarian context and inhabitants as holdovers from a bygone era. As a result, it misses what we might call the conditions of ‘extended agrarian urbanisation’. Here, too, the conditions can be compared with more apposite cases than Pudong, such as the old district of Thủ Thiêm in Ho Chi Minh City. As urban anthropologist Erik Harms argues, the nature of such coalitional demands, and the tensions within them, are important for addressing such questions. 

In Thủ Thiêm, residents’ claims for securing better land and property prices within an expanding neoliberal (urban) economy underpinned the apparent inevitability of their eventual displacement (Erik Harms, Luxury and Rubble: Civility and Dispossession in the New Saigon, Oakland, CA, 2016. For a related discussion of ‘sellers’ remorse’ in Gurgaon, India, see Sarasji Majumder and Subhra Gururani, ‘Land as an Intermittent Commodity: Ethnographic Insights from India’s Urban–Agrarian Frontiers’, Urbanisation, 6(1), 2021, pp. 49–63).
A woman and her granddaughter stand among uprooted trees on land cleared for a housing project in Kaliganj, Gazipur. Such transformations raise questions about the livelihoods and economic prospects of displaced landowners, smallholding farmers and tenants. The photo was taken in August 2013. Photo: Rashed Sumon

We can see similar appeals mobilised by land brokers and sellers in Kanchon and across Greater Dhaka, where displacement becomes a normalised aspect of urban development, including through the workings of land acquisition laws. The 2017 land acquisition act, for instance, retains a provision under which a dispute over a land transaction below a certain landholding threshold cannot be appealed to authorities above the district level or taken to civil courts (Part II, provisions 4 and 5. Section 4[3(a) and (b)] of the 1982 ordinance had set limits on how far up the administrative chain an objection against acquisition could go, based on landholding size. A 1994 amendment provided that district-level officials would determine whether an objection to an acquisition would be heard for holdings of six acres or less, which is far higher than the average landholding in this region. Moreover, section 5[2] left it to the discretion of district officials whether land acquisition for public projects would proceed, as well as whether compensation would be provided to tenants and sharecroppers, without any provision for appeal to civil courts. The 2017 repeal of this ordinance and its replacement by a new act retained these provisions, with minor changes intended to bring compensation levels closer to purportedly market-determined rates). While facilitating better prices for larger landowners, it removes a recourse, however imperfect, for smallholders against the collusive power of local officials and land brokers in price negotiations. 

Comparing such agrarian contexts of extended urbanisation across Indian cases, including the role of the state and legal regimes, might be more productive here (see Sai Balakrishnan and Subhra Gururani, ‘New Terrains of Agrarian–Urban Studies: Limits and Possibilities’, Urbanisation, 6(1), 2021, pp. 7–15, for an excellent special issue on these themes in the Indian context. Also see Sai Balakrishnan, Shareholder Cities: Land Transformations Along Urban Corridors in India, Philadelphia, PA, 2019). Projected growth rates along ‘economic corridors’ can then be evaluated alongside social and ecological costs, from displacement to waterlogging, to make these visions count towards planning perspectives that are both broader and fairer than the one articulated in the report. It is a case in which the ‘vision’ itself, rather than a lack of it, becomes part of the problem. And since these visions depend on our comparative frames, the question ‘which east?’ requires careful consideration.

Mushahid Hussain is an academic and researcher trained in historical sociology and political economy. He holds a PhD in Development Sociology from Cornell University and is currently a faculty member at Trinity College.

Here, too, the conditions can be compared with more apposite cases than Pudong, such as the old district of Thủ Thiêm in Ho Chi Minh City. As urban anthropologist Erik Harms argues, the nature of such coalitional demands, and the tensions within them, are important for addressing such questions. 

In Thủ Thiêm, residents’ claims for securing better land and property prices within an expanding neoliberal (urban) economy underpinned the apparent inevitability of their eventual displacement (Erik Harms, Luxury and Rubble: Civility and Dispossession in the New Saigon, Oakland, CA, 2016. A woman and her granddaughter stand among uprooted trees on land cleared for a housing project in Kaliganj, Gazipur. Such transformations raise questions about the livelihoods and economic prospects of displaced landowners, smallholding farmers and tenants. The photo was taken in August 2013. Photo: Rashed Sumon

The 2017 land acquisition act, for instance, retains a provision under which a dispute over a land transaction below a certain landholding threshold cannot be appealed to authorities above the district level or taken to civil courts (Part II, provisions 4 and 5. Section 4[3(a) and (b)] of the 1982 ordinance had set limits on how far up the administrative chain an objection against acquisition could go, based on landholding size. A 1994 amendment provided that district-level officials would determine whether an objection to an acquisition would be heard for holdings of six acres or less, which is far higher than the average landholding in this region. Moreover, section 5[2] left it to the discretion of district officials whether land acquisition for public projects would proceed, as well as whether compensation would be provided to tenants and sharecroppers, without any provision for appeal to civil courts. The 2017 repeal of this ordinance and its replacement by a new act retained these provisions, with minor changes intended to bring compensation levels closer to purportedly market-determined rates). It is a case in which the ‘vision’ itself, rather than a lack of it, becomes part of the problem. And since these visions depend on our comparative frames, the question ‘which east?’ requires careful consideration.

item.title: The Daily Star – Bangladesh–Malaysia labour migration: Can the new initiative break the cycle of exploitation?
item.description:
It is encouraging that labour migration from Bangladesh to Malaysia is likely to resume at the end of this month. However, given the history of repeated suspensions, a more important question is whether this renewed initiative will address the structural problems that have long plagued the recruitment process.

Malaysia has suspended labour recruitment from Bangladesh several times: first in the 1990s, then between 2008 and 2012, again from 2019 to 2022, and most recently in May 2024. The recurring allegations behind these suspensions include corruption in recruitment, exorbitant migration costs, indebtedness, unemployment and severe exploitation of migrant workers.

To address these problems, particularly excessive migration costs and the resulting indebtedness, both governments have repeatedly experimented with alternative recruitment mechanisms. In 2012, Bangladesh and Malaysia signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to recruit workers through a government-to-government (G2G) mechanism. Despite considerable interest among prospective migrants, only a small number could migrate because of limited institutional capacity and delays in the recruitment process on both sides. The initiative failed to achieve its target of recruiting 30,000 workers.

In 2016, the two countries attempted to revive the initiative through a G2G-Plus mechanism, incorporating private recruiting agencies. Approximately 160,000 Bangladeshi workers migrated to Malaysia under this arrangement. However, the system gradually became vulnerable to malpractice. Bangladesh effectively handed control of the recruitment process and worker departures to a handful of influential recruiting agencies. Allegations of corruption and excessive migration fees emerged, with these agencies reportedly making substantial profits at the expense of prospective migrants.

A new MoU was signed in December 2021. However, no workers could depart until August 2022 because the two countries failed to agree on recruitment modalities. Concerns grew that influential actors on both sides were attempting to establish another recruitment syndicate. These concerns intensified when Malaysian Human Resources Minister M Saravanan visited Bangladesh and indicated that only 25 Bangladeshi recruiting agencies would be permitted to send workers.

This raised serious questions about the commitment to reform. Allowing a limited number of agencies to control recruitment risked reproducing the very system that had contributed to the previous suspension in 2019. Industry insiders alleged that a powerful group of 25 agencies was using its financial and political influence to persuade authorities in both countries to grant it exclusive access to the market, enabling them to profit from financially vulnerable migrant workers.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim shakes hands with Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman during a welcoming ceremony in Putrajaya, Malaysia, on 22 June 2026. During the visit, both countries agreed to review their existing labour recruitment agreement and work towards a new one, pledging to ensure transparent, fair and competitive recruitment. Photo: Anwar Ibrahim/Facebook

The problem, however, extends beyond recruitment agencies. Malaysia's labour migration governance has been affected by corruption, powerful recruitment intermediaries, exploitative employer practices and loopholes in existing laws and regulations.

Labour migration eventually resumed in August 2022. Malaysian authorities initially selected only 25 Bangladeshi recruiting agencies. However, the Bangladesh government, working with the United Nations and the International Labour Organization (ILO), persuaded Malaysia to expand the list. In 2023, the number of authorised agencies increased to 101. Despite this expansion, migration costs remained considerably higher than the desired level. Between August 2022 and May 2024, approximately 500,000 Bangladeshi workers migrated to Malaysia through the selected agencies. Yet, in May 2024, Malaysia again suspended recruitment, citing essentially the same concerns that had prompted previous suspensions.

This recurring pattern raises a fundamental question: why have successive recruitment arrangements failed to establish a transparent, affordable and accountable migration system?

Under the latest initiative, labour migration from Bangladesh is expected to resume in November, 2026. Initially, some workers will be recruited through the state-owned Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), reportedly at no cost to workers. The government's target of sending 10,000 workers through this arrangement is commendable. However, experience suggests that achieving this target may not be straightforward.

While government-to-government recruitment can protect workers against excessive fees, it is unlikely to meet the growing demand for overseas employment on its own. A well-regulated private recruitment sector will remain essential. The challenge is to ensure that private agencies operate within a transparent and competitive framework rather than allowing a handful of influential players to dominate the market.

Under the proposed arrangement, Malaysia has again selected 25 principal recruiting agencies while allowing an additional 312 agencies to operate as associate agencies. It remains uncertain whether this structure will resolve the problems that led to previous suspensions. 

If Malaysia introduces a technology-enabled, integrated monitoring system, there should be little justification for restricting recruitment to a small number of principal agencies. Such a platform could connect local employers, recruitment agencies and immigration authorities, enabling authorities to monitor job offers, recruitment approvals, fees and worker departures.
Bangladeshi workers queue at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka before departing for Malaysia under a government-to-government recruitment arrangement in August 2013. Photo: Star

Malaysia could also learn from other labour-receiving countries in Southeast Asia and Europe. One underlying problem is the failure to regulate employers effectively. Some employers reportedly demand more workers than they actually need, while fraudulent job offers create mismatches between labour demand and supply. This can result in unemployment and wider social problems. Such management failures cannot be resolved by monopolising recruitment. A well-regulated and competitive system can reduce migration costs, improve worker-employer matching and ensure recruitment reflects genuine labour market demand.

The Bangladesh government has also taken an important step by setting a ceiling of Tk 154,000 for migration costs. This is a positive step, but its success will depend on proper monitoring and strict enforcement. Bangladesh has had similar experiences before. In 2017, the government fixed maximum migration costs for different destination countries. For example, the prescribed cost for Saudi Arabia was Tk 165,000. Yet, in practice, many workers reportedly paid Tk 600,000 to Tk 700,000 to secure employment abroad. This gap illustrates the limitations of administrative price controls without effective enforcement.

The lesson from successive suspensions of labour migration to Malaysia is clear: changing recruitment arrangements or introducing new cost ceilings will not be enough. Unless both governments address market concentration, eliminate excessive intermediary charges, regulate employers and establish effective accountability mechanisms, the same problems are likely to resurface.

For Bangladesh, overseas employment is not merely a source of foreign exchange; it is a vital livelihood opportunity for millions of households. Protecting migrant workers must therefore be at the centre of any bilateral recruitment agreement. The success of the proposed reopening should not be measured simply by how many workers leave Bangladesh, but by how many secure genuine employment without falling into debt or facing exploitation. Breaking this recurring cycle must be the real objective.

Professor Dr Md Bakhtiar Uddin is Head of the Department of Economics at Jatiya Kabi Kazi Nazrul Islam University, Trishal, Mymensingh. He can be reached at [email protected].

item.title: The Daily Star – Do Bangladesh and India still need the Ganges Treaty?
item.description:
The Ganges Water Sharing Treaty expires on 12 December. Thirty years of joint observation and allocation at Farakka will end with it unless something takes their place, and the record those thirty years have produced has not been closely examined in public.

It is worth reading because almost every finding in it contradicts something believed in one capital or the other. The allocation formula was implemented better than the argument in Dhaka assumes. The river's gain between the two gauges is real, but it has never been quantified publicly. And the alternating ten-day guarantee that both governments treat as the treaty's central protective mechanism largely does not survive the journey downstream, so it is not doing what either believes. The numbers that follow come from the public record. The narratives depend on who is reading and how.

The record, and one caveat about it

The record covers 450 ten-day periods: thirty dry seasons from 1997 to 2026, fifteen periods each from 1 January to 31 May. Every period carries four quantities: total flow available at Farakka, the release to India, the release to Bangladesh, and the flow observed at Hardinge Bridge, downstream inside Bangladesh and below the Mahananda confluence. The data come from the Joint Rivers Commission's published record.

One caveat belongs at the beginning rather than in a footnote because it limits what can objectively be claimed from the record.

In all 450 periods over the last 30 years, availability at Farakka is exactly the sum of the two releases. Availability is therefore an accounting quantity, not an independent measurement, so testing whether the releases followed the formula shows that an agreed account is internally consistent. It does not confirm what the river actually did.

The Hardinge Bridge observation sits outside this availability accounting.
What reaches Hardinge Bridge, as a ratio of what was released at Farakka, for each ten day period of the dry season. Source: Joint Rivers Commission records, 1997-2026 (450 ten day periods)

What the formula delivered

Of 450 releases to Bangladesh, 375 were within 0.5 cusec of the formula applied to recorded availability, and 384 within 1 cusec. Twenty periods fell more than 1 cusec short, three of them by more than 100. One period in thirty years breached the ninety-per-cent threshold of Article XI: 1–10 April 1997, with a shortfall of 4,863 cusec. There is no shortfall above 1 cusec anywhere in the record after 2003. Departures favoured Bangladesh: 3.66 billion cubic metres of surplus against 0.143 billion cubic metres of shortfall. These are observed figures. Two qualifications matter before they become a story.

One year accounts for most of the surplus. 2012 alone accounts for 2.15 of the 3.66 billion cubic metres: from January to early March that year, India took 21,000 to 32,000 cusecs instead of 40,000, which suggests a feeder-canal or barrage constraint rather than a concession. Hardinge Bridge, moreover, recorded less than the release in six of those seven periods, so the recorded surplus barely appears downstream. Set 2012 aside and the ratio falls from about 25 to one to about 10 to one: still in Bangladesh's favour, but a different claim. Only the Joint Committee's operating records could settle which explanation is correct, and they are not public.

Availability shows no trend. It was tested in four ways: the whole dry season, the critical period, the rest of the season, and the annual minimum. None shows a statistically significant trend. So the claim that India has been taking progressively more is not supported by this record. Neither is the claim that flows are stable: thirty seasons cannot separate a slow change from year-to-year variation, and the 2007–2016 decade ran some eight per cent below the decades on either side. A thirty-year treaty can contain a dry decade that its own trend test cannot detect.

How much the river adds

Between Farakka and Hardinge Bridge, the river gains water: from the Mahananda, from groundwater, and from irrigation return flows. That much is uncontested, and it forms the basis of a claim now circulating in Indian commentary: that Bangladesh already receives more than the treaty gives it, and that renewal should adjust the shares accordingly. An analysis using the same Joint Rivers Commission data observes that flows at Hardinge Bridge have generally been higher than releases at Farakka, and interprets this as favouring upstream India in hydrodiplomacy. The analysis does not quantify the gain. Bangladeshi accounts, for their part, tend not to mention the gain at all. The record is unkind to both.

The relationship between Farakka and Hardinge Bridge is strong. The river gains water between these two locations and gains proportionally more when flows are high. At the median, the gain is about 11 per cent. The gain is also not uniform. The higher range occurs in January, when flows are heavy. During the critical period from 11 March to 10 May, the gain stops increasing with flow, and in Bangladesh's own guarantee periods, it vanishes altogether. Hardinge Bridge recorded less than the Farakka release in 88 of 450 periods, with a mean deficit of 3,728 cusec and a maximum of 15,098. Eighty-eight periods out of 450 are not a rounding error in a claim about downstream abundance.
Hardinge Bridge in Pabna. The bridge is a crucial monitoring point for Ganges flows entering Bangladesh, providing data that help assess the downstream effects of water releases at Farakka. Photo: Star

The alternating guarantee

Under Annexure I, each country is guaranteed 35,000 cusec in three alternating ten-day periods between 11 March and 10 May. Bangladesh's are the second period of March and the first and third periods of April; India's are the third period of March, the second period of April and the first period of May, as the indicative schedule in Annexure II sets out. This alternation is the treaty's central protective mechanism.

11 March – 10 MayMean release at FarakkaMean at Hardinge BridgePeriods with Hardinge Bridge below release
Bangladesh's guarantee periods38,64240,16839 of 90
India's guarantee periods33,40839,79510 of 90
Within-year paired difference+5,234+373—

 

Bangladesh's guarantee periods raise the release at Farakka by 5,234 cusec. At Hardinge Bridge, that becomes 373 cusec, statistically indistinguishable from zero. Even in the periods when the guarantee actually increased Bangladesh's release, only about a fifth of the extra water arrived. The periods when Hardinge Bridge records less than the release occur almost four times as often during Bangladesh's own guarantee periods: 39 of 90, compared with 10 of 90 during India's.

The reason is that the river smooths out the alternation. What arrives at Hardinge Bridge tracks roughly the average of the current and preceding releases, rather than the current release alone. Travel time, channel storage and the averaging of ten-day figures could all produce this effect, and a difference in measurement timing between the two stations cannot be ruled out.

This is not an argument about generosity or compliance, and the implication runs in both directions. A protection designed around alternating ten-day pulses at Farakka is largely erased by the river before the water reaches the stretch where Bangladesh uses it. Dhaka treats that guarantee as the protection it most needs to restore; Delhi treats it as a commitment it would rather not formalise. On this record, neither position is accurate. The guarantee delivers very little additional water to where Bangladesh uses it, and an argument about strengthening or resisting it is an argument about something largely notional.
A large stretch of the Mahananda River near the Bir Shreshtha Captain Mohiuddin Jahangir Bridge in Chapainawabganj lies dry, exposing land used for paddy cultivation in 2015. A tributary of the Padma, the river faces recurring dry-season water shortages attributed to upstream barrages in India, including Farakka.

The consultation threshold

The treaty contains a second protective mechanism. Article II provides for immediate consultations between the two governments when availability at Farakka falls below 50,000 cusec.

In 450 periods, that threshold was crossed only once: 21–31 March 1997, at 48,487 cusec.

Whatever one thinks of consultation as an instrument, a trigger set at that level would have operated only once in thirty years. Neither government has published an analysis of how often a strengthened provision would be triggered.

Where the disagreement actually is

Set the transmission question aside, and the remaining disagreement is not about numbers at all. It is about where the risk of uncertainty and a changing climate should lie: upstream, downstream or shared through a formula.

The argument against a volumetric guarantee is sound as far as it goes: an unconditional fixed volume places climate risk on the upstream party. Bangladesh could argue that, as the downstream party, it already bears the consequences of every shortfall. Both propositions are true. Which one should prevail is a question of values, and no dataset can settle it. Acknowledging this is not a concession; it is the precondition for arguing about design rather than motive. Principled pragmatism begins here: not by splitting the difference, but by separating the questions that data can resolve from those they cannot.

It holds that strict adherence to principle without pragmatism is usually not actionable, and that pragmatism without principle is neither sustainable nor equitable. The operating rule that follows is narrow and useful: compromise over interests is possible and actionable, while compromising principles is not. The task, therefore, is not to establish the truth about the Ganges, but to agree on a truth that is negotiable and implementable, given the capacity, constraints and context the two countries actually face.
An aerial view of the Padma River reveals extensive sandbars exposed by declining dry-season flows, highlighting concerns over water availability downstream of the Farakka Barrage. Photo: Rashed Shumon

Applied here, the dispute reorganises itself. Whether India or Bangladesh should bear the risk of a drier future is a question of principle, and neither capital will concede it before 12 December. Whether the alternating guarantee transmits downstream is a question of fact, and the record answers it: largely, it does not. That answer is useful precisely because it favours neither party. It tells Dhaka that its central demand, as presently designed, would deliver little of what is being sought; it tells Delhi that the commitment it is reluctant to formalise would transfer very little additional water downstream. An argument over principle becomes an argument over instrument design, which is more tractable.

The same logic dissolves the apparent either-or options. Bangladesh needs dry-season reliability; India needs protection against committing to volumes that a changing climate may not deliver. The 1996 treaty treated these as alternatives and split the difference by alternating ten-day pulses, which, as the record shows, delivered neither. A percentage floor within a schedule that adjusts to availability is one instrument that could address both concerns, because it is contingent by construction: it does not require any particular climate future to materialise. Whether it is the best instrument is a separate question, and one this record cannot settle. What the record does establish is what principled pragmatism demands of any instrument: not optimality, but a resolution that still works when the assumptions behind it fail.

What ends on 12 December

Water diplomacy starts with a question that seems trivial: what is one plus one? The answer depends on who is asked and why. These 450 records support Delhi's reading that Bangladesh already receives more than the treaty gives it, and Dhaka's reading that the dry season is short. Both interpretations are present in the data. Neither is complete. Setting them side by side is the first step, because two parties reasoning from the same numbers to opposite conclusions cannot negotiate until they understand why.

The second question is where to intervene. Measurement is not negotiable; what is negotiable is the point at which a change affects the system. On this record, that point is not the volume at Farakka, which both capitals have contested for thirty years. It is where, and over what period, a guarantee is defined. A pulse that exists at the barrage but not at Hardinge Bridge is not an allocation problem but a design problem, and design problems allow for more solutions.

The third is the hardest: when positions are entrenched, look for the eighteenth camel, the borrowed thing that makes an indivisible problem divisible and is returned once the problem is resolved. Here, that is measurement itself. The one finding neither side can explain alone is that the gain between the two stations is growing by roughly 2,000 cusec per decade. It could be tributary inflow, a changed rating curve or channel change, and nobody can say which, though each possibility carries different consequences for the two parties. No unilateral record can distinguish between them. Joint observation could, and the answer could just as easily vindicate Delhi as Dhaka: if the growing gain comes from tributary inflow, the river is delivering more than the treaty allocates, which is what Indian commentary contends. It costs neither country water and concedes nothing on who should bear climate risk.
The Farakka Barrage in India, where the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty regulates dry-season water allocation between India and Bangladesh. File photo

That observation falls under the Joint Committee, a body established under Article IV. If the treaty lapses on 12 December with nothing in its place, the mandate lapses with it, and the 2027 dry season becomes the first since 1996 without joint measurements.

India and Bangladesh agree on very little about this river. For thirty years, they measured it the same way anyway, and every finding above exists because they did. Measurement allocates no water, which is why it is the easiest thing on the renewal table to preserve. It is also why losing it would be the hardest of the losses on 12 December to justify. The treaty does end on its own terms. But the Joint Rivers Commission, which predates it by twenty-four years, does not, and nothing prevents the two governments from keeping the gauges operating under that older mandate while they work out what replaces the rest.

Shafiqul Islam is a professor of Engineering and Diplomacy at Tufts University, where he directs the Water Diplomacy Program and teaches at the School of Engineering and the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy. He is a 2025–26 Radcliffe Fellow at Harvard University.

Neither is the claim that flows are stable: thirty seasons cannot separate a slow change from year-to-year variation, and the 2007–2016 decade ran some eight per cent below the decades on either side. A thirty-year treaty can contain a dry decade that its own trend test cannot detect.

How much the river adds

Between Farakka and Hardinge Bridge, the river gains water: from the Mahananda, from groundwater, and from irrigation return flows. That much is uncontested, and it forms the basis of a claim now circulating in Indian commentary: that Bangladesh already receives more than the treaty gives it, and that renewal should adjust the shares accordingly. An analysis using the same Joint Rivers Commission data observes that flows at Hardinge Bridge have generally been higher than releases at Farakka, and interprets this as favouring upstream India in hydrodiplomacy. The analysis does not quantify the gain. Bangladeshi accounts, for their part, tend not to mention the gain at all. The record is unkind to both.

The relationship between Farakka and Hardinge Bridge is strong. The river gains water between these two locations and gains proportionally more when flows are high. At the median, the gain is about 11 per cent. The gain is also not uniform. The higher range occurs in January, when flows are heavy. During the critical period from 11 March to 10 May, the gain stops increasing with flow, and in Bangladesh's own guarantee periods, it vanishes altogether. Hardinge Bridge recorded less than the Farakka release in 88 of 450 periods, with a mean deficit of 3,728 cusec and a maximum of 15,098. Eighty-eight periods out of 450 are not a rounding error in a claim about downstream abundance.
Hardinge Bridge in Pabna. The bridge is a crucial monitoring point for Ganges flows entering Bangladesh, providing data that help assess the downstream effects of water releases at Farakka. Photo: Star

The alternating guarantee

Under Annexure I, each country is guaranteed 35,000 cusec in three alternating ten-day periods between 11 March and 10 May. Bangladesh's are the second period of March and the first and third periods of April; India's are the third period of March, the second period of April and the first period of May, as the indicative schedule in Annexure II sets out. This alternation is the treaty's central protective mechanism.

11 March – 10 MayMean release at FarakkaMean at Hardinge BridgePeriods with Hardinge Bridge below release
Bangladesh's guarantee periods38,64240,16839 of 90
India's guarantee periods33,40839,79510 of 90
Within-year paired difference+5,234+373—

 

Bangladesh's guarantee periods raise the release at Farakka by 5,234 cusec. At Hardinge Bridge, that becomes 373 cusec, statistically indistinguishable from zero. Even in the periods when the guarantee actually increased Bangladesh's release, only about a fifth of the extra water arrived. The periods when Hardinge Bridge records less than the release occur almost four times as often during Bangladesh's own guarantee periods: 39 of 90, compared with 10 of 90 during India's.

The reason is that the river smooths out the alternation. What arrives at Hardinge Bridge tracks roughly the average of the current and preceding releases, rather than the current release alone. Travel time, channel storage and the averaging of ten-day figures could all produce this effect, and a difference in measurement timing between the two stations cannot be ruled out.

This is not an argument about generosity or compliance, and the implication runs in both directions. A protection designed around alternating ten-day pulses at Farakka is largely erased by the river before the water reaches the stretch where Bangladesh uses it. Dhaka treats that guarantee as the protection it most needs to restore; Delhi treats it as a commitment it would rather not formalise. On this record, neither position is accurate. The guarantee delivers very little additional water to where Bangladesh uses it, and an argument about strengthening or resisting it is an argument about something largely notional.
A large stretch of the Mahananda River near the Bir Shreshtha Captain Mohiuddin Jahangir Bridge in Chapainawabganj lies dry, exposing land used for paddy cultivation in 2015. A tributary of the Padma, the river faces recurring dry-season water shortages attributed to upstream barrages in India, including Farakka.

The consultation threshold

The treaty contains a second protective mechanism. Article II provides for immediate consultations between the two governments when availability at Farakka falls below 50,000 cusec.

In 450 periods, that threshold was crossed only once: 21–31 March 1997, at 48,487 cusec.

Whatever one thinks of consultation as an instrument, a trigger set at that level would have operated only once in thirty years. Neither government has published an analysis of how often a strengthened provision would be triggered.

Where the disagreement actually is

Set the transmission question aside, and the remaining disagreement is not about numbers at all. It is about where the risk of uncertainty and a changing climate should lie: upstream, downstream or shared through a formula.

The argument against a volumetric guarantee is sound as far as it goes: an unconditional fixed volume places climate risk on the upstream party. Bangladesh could argue that, as the downstream party, it already bears the consequences of every shortfall. Both propositions are true. Which one should prevail is a question of values, and no dataset can settle it. Acknowledging this is not a concession; it is the precondition for arguing about design rather than motive. Principled pragmatism begins here: not by splitting the difference, but by separating the questions that data can resolve from those they cannot.

It holds that strict adherence to principle without pragmatism is usually not actionable, and that pragmatism without principle is neither sustainable nor equitable. The operating rule that follows is narrow and useful: compromise over interests is possible and actionable, while compromising principles is not. The task, therefore, is not to establish the truth about the Ganges, but to agree on a truth that is negotiable and implementable, given the capacity, constraints and context the two countries actually face.
An aerial view of the Padma River reveals extensive sandbars exposed by declining dry-season flows, highlighting concerns over water availability downstream of the Farakka Barrage. Photo: Rashed Shumon

Applied here, the dispute reorganises itself. Whether India or Bangladesh should bear the risk of a drier future is a question of principle, and neither capital will concede it before 12 December. Whether the alternating guarantee transmits downstream is a question of fact, and the record answers it: largely, it does not. That answer is useful precisely because it favours neither party. It tells Dhaka that its central demand, as presently designed, would deliver little of what is being sought; it tells Delhi that the commitment it is reluctant to formalise would transfer very little additional water downstream. An argument over principle becomes an argument over instrument design, which is more tractable.

The same logic dissolves the apparent either-or options. Bangladesh needs dry-season reliability; India needs protection against committing to volumes that a changing climate may not deliver. The 1996 treaty treated these as alternatives and split the difference by alternating ten-day pulses, which, as the record shows, delivered neither. A percentage floor within a schedule that adjusts to availability is one instrument that could address both concerns, because it is contingent by construction: it does not require any particular climate future to materialise. Whether it is the best instrument is a separate question, and one this record cannot settle. What the record does establish is what principled pragmatism demands of any instrument: not optimality, but a resolution that still works when the assumptions behind it fail.

What ends on 12 December

Water diplomacy starts with a question that seems trivial: what is one plus one? The answer depends on who is asked and why. These 450 records support Delhi's reading that Bangladesh already receives more than the treaty gives it, and Dhaka's reading that the dry season is short. Both interpretations are present in the data. Neither is complete. Setting them side by side is the first step, because two parties reasoning from the same numbers to opposite conclusions cannot negotiate until they understand why.

The second question is where to intervene. Measurement is not negotiable; what is negotiable is the point at which a change affects the system. On this record, that point is not the volume at Farakka, which both capitals have contested for thirty years. It is where, and over what period, a guarantee is defined. A pulse that exists at the barrage but not at Hardinge Bridge is not an allocation problem but a design problem, and design problems allow for more solutions.

The third is the hardest: when positions are entrenched, look for the eighteenth camel, the borrowed thing that makes an indivisible problem divisible and is returned once the problem is resolved. Here, that is measurement itself. The one finding neither side can explain alone is that the gain between the two stations is growing by roughly 2,000 cusec per decade. It could be tributary inflow, a changed rating curve or channel change, and nobody can say which, though each possibility carries different consequences for the two parties. No unilateral record can distinguish between them. Joint observation could, and the answer could just as easily vindicate Delhi as Dhaka: if the growing gain comes from tributary inflow, the river is delivering more than the treaty allocates, which is what Indian commentary contends. It costs neither country water and concedes nothing on who should bear climate risk.
The Farakka Barrage in India, where the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty regulates dry-season water allocation between India and Bangladesh. File photo

That observation falls under the Joint Committee, a body established under Article IV. If the treaty lapses on 12 December with nothing in its place, the mandate lapses with it, and the 2027 dry season becomes the first since 1996 without joint measurements.

India and Bangladesh agree on very little about this river. For thirty years, they measured it the same way anyway, and every finding above exists because they did. Measurement allocates no water, which is why it is the easiest thing on the renewal table to preserve. It is also why losing it would be the hardest of the losses on 12 December to justify. The treaty does end on its own terms. But the Joint Rivers Commission, which predates it by twenty-four years, does not, and nothing prevents the two governments from keeping the gauges operating under that older mandate while they work out what replaces the rest.

Shafiqul Islam is a professor of Engineering and Diplomacy at Tufts University, where he directs the Water Diplomacy Program and teaches at the School of Engineering and the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy. He is a 2025–26 Radcliffe Fellow at Harvard University.

item.title: The Daily Star – The hidden costs of our dependence on Microsoft
item.description:
When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations.

Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence?

We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences.

As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so much of it depends on a handful of technology companies?

The cloud has a physical footprint

The cloud may sound weightless, but it runs on data centres, electricity, cooling systems and hardware.

The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres consumed 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, around 1.5% of global demand. It projects that consumption could reach 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, largely driven by AI and other digital services.

Microsoft’s own 2026 sustainability report illustrates the tension. The company reported a 25% year-over-year rise in total emissions in 2025, primarily because of expanding data centres and a change in renewable-energy certificate accounting. Microsoft is also investing in cleaner energy and more efficient infrastructure. Both facts matter: technological progress can reduce emissions per task, while growth pushes overall demand higher.

Asking the right questions

Turkey’s Cop31 presidency released the voluntary Antalya artificial intelligence pledge in October. This pledge aims to encourage climate-responsible AI while acknowledging the energy and water demands of the technology.

The World Resources Institute, a global research organisation, welcomed the pledge’s direction but warned that voluntary commitments need stronger accountability mechanisms. Meanwhile, the International Telecommunication Union has scheduled a Cop31 event for November 16 on financing cleaner digital infrastructure, measuring emissions, and promoting durable, repairable and reusable electronics.

The message is important: sustainability cannot stop at greener electricity. It also concerns what technology organisations purchase, how long they keep it, and who pays for its environmental effects. 
 
Microsoft products including Outlook were out of action globally on November 13 2026. Alex Photo Stock/Shutterstock

When a software decision becomes a hardware bill

Consider a computer that still works but cannot support a newer operating system. Windows 10’s regular support ended in October 2025, although Microsoft offers extended security updates for eligible consumer devices through October 2027.

The transition does not make every older computer obsolete. Yet software support and compatibility can influence whether organisations replace otherwise usable equipment.

Manufacturing devices consumes energy and raw materials. It also creates electronic waste (e-waste). According to the UN’s global e-waste monitor, the world generated 62 million metric tonnes of e-waste in 2022, of which just 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled.

These figures cover all electronic waste, not waste attributable to Microsoft. They nevertheless show why extending equipment lifetimes deserves a place in climate policy.

Costs that are rarely counted

A software subscription has a visible price. Less visible are the costs of training employees, migrating files, replacing equipment, maintaining duplicate systems and eventually switching suppliers.

Economists call these switching costs. They can lock organisations into existing providers even when better-value alternatives emerge.

This is not merely hypothetical. In March 2026, the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority announced plans to investigate Microsoft’s business software ecosystem. It also reported steps by major cloud service providers, including Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services, to reduce data-transfer fees and improve interoperability, making it easier for businesses to switch between providers.

What might this have to do with sustainability? A buyer unable to change providers easily may also struggle to choose lower-emission computing services. That is a potential environmental consequence of lock-in, not a demonstrated claim that Microsoft users emit more carbon.

There is a wider accounting problem too. The UN estimates that global electronic waste was associated with approximately US$78 billion (£59 billion) in externalised costs in 2022, including pollution and climate-related impacts. Such costs are largely absent from the price of a software license.

A responsible procurement decision should therefore compare lifetime financial costs, equipment lifespans and credible emissions data rather than only the next annual bill.

Freedom to choose

Could workplaces use alternatives (such as Thunderbird and LibreOffice) or interoperable cloud services? Often, yes. But migration has costs and a rival provider is not necessarily greener.

The better goal is freedom to choose: portable data, open document formats, repairable devices, transparent environmental reporting and software contracts that do not penalise switching.

Digital systems that remain affordable, competitive and environmentally responsible, even when their preferred technology changes, will be the most resilient ones.

This article was first published under the title “Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence.” in The Conversation, on November 13, 2026.

Narmin Nahidi is an assistant Professor in Finance, University of Exeter.

item.title: The Daily Star – Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq: Revisiting a complex legacy
item.description: One of the most influential political figures in the history of Bengal, Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq left an enduring legacy through his advocacy for peasant rights, his challenge to entrenched political and economic power, and his role in shaping the politics of colonial and postcolonial Bengal. Yet his political thought, achievements and contradictions deserve renewed attention beyond familiar historical narratives. Through a collection of essays and historical analyses, The Daily Star's Slow Reads revisits his life, political struggles, ideas and legacy, exploring how his vision and actions shaped Bengal's past and continue to resonate in Bangladesh today.
